title: MB8-25482
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): She is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated October 4, 2018, rejecting her refugee protection claim.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Haiti. She is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated October 4, 2018, rejecting her refugee protection claim. The RPD rejected the appellant's testimony because it lacked credibility. It concluded that the main allegations in her refugee protection claim are not credible. The RPD found that significant omissions and contradictions between the appellant's Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), the amended version of it and her testimony at the hearing were not explained in a satisfactory manner. The RPD also concluded that the appellant did not show that she would face a serious possibility of persecution by reason of her membership in the particular social group of Haitian women.

The appellant is asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to set aside the RPD's determination and to allow her appeal. She essentially states that the RPD rendered a decision based on erroneous conclusions in fact and in law drawn in a perverse and capricious manner or without taking into account all the information that was available, which is inconsistent with the objective and spirit of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). The appellant argues that the RPD made palpable errors in finding that she was not credible.

In this appeal, the RAD must determine whether the RPD erred in its assessment of the appellant's credibility. After a full and independent analysis of the evidence presented, I conclude that the RPD's decision was correct and that it did not err in its assessment.
Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, I confirm the RPD's determination that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. I dismiss the appeal.

In her memorandum of appeal, the appellant states that she is afraid of returning to Haiti for fear of being targeted by her husband and the police. On XXXX XXXX, 2009, she left the country to attend her father's funeral in the United States. She had a residence permit, so she stayed and completed a XXXX training while financially supporting her family members who were still in Haiti and had been affected by the 2010 earthquake. Her family was being extorted by the police. When she learned that her husband was cheating on her, the appellant returned to Haiti and caught him in the act of adultery, and her husband reacted violently. The appellant went back to the United States, but because the current administration did not want to extend her permanent status, she came to Canada, and she made a claim for refugee protection on July 5, 2017.

On questions of fact, law, and mixed fact and law, the RAD applied the correctness standard, in accordance with the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Huruglica.1 I will therefore conduct my own analysis of the record, which includes listening to the recording of the hearing, to determine whether the RPD erred. ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL Breach of procedural fairness and natural justice
paragraphs.heading_before: ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

paragraphs.text: The appellant submits that the RPD's conclusions clearly constitute a breach of natural justice and procedural fairness. According to her, the RPD asked her questions at the hearing for the purpose of identifying contradictions and inconsistencies between her BOC Form signed on July 5, 2018, and the amended version of it filed on September 17, 2018. Her amendments were prepared to modify the BOC Form that had been prepared, translated and filed by her former counsel.2 The appellant submits that the RPD intentionally looked for problems between the two versions of her BOC Form and her testimony.

I find that the RPD took the right approach by informing the appellant about the problems with her written account, giving her the opportunity to explain herself, analyzing her answer and drawing the appropriate conclusions while explaining their impact on her credibility.

The RPD noticed that there were major omissions, contradictions and inconsistencies between the BOC Form that the appellant signed on July 5, 2018, and the one she filed on September 17, 2018, barely three days prior to her hearing. The appellant testified at the hearing that she fears the Haitian police, her husband and his mistress.3 She stated that since XXXX XXXX, 2014, she has feared the Haitian police because there is no justice for women. When the RPD asked her to elaborate, she testified that while she was in the United States, the money that she was sending to her mother in Haiti was being extorted by the police at the request of her husband, who has friends in the police department, so he and the police could share it. She failed to mention in her BOC Form that her husband was involved in the extortion by the police and that her problems with him were the reason why the police were extorting her mother. The appellant also failed to mention any fear of her husband in her BOC Form. According to the changes made to her BOC Form three days prior to the hearing, her husband was actually the victim of extortion attempts by the police. In my opinion, there are three versions of the facts that contradict each other.

The RPD made the effort to inform the appellant of these elements and asked her about them. I note that on several occasions, it made the effort to summarize the appellant's words and have her confirm that this was what she had meant. The RPD gave her the opportunity to explain herself.

The RPD tried asking the appellant why such serious allegations were omitted from her BOC Form and the amendments she made three days prior to the hearing, and why those documents did not reflect the version given at the hearing.4 The appellant blamed the person who translated her BOC Form, noting that she is not responsible for the translation.

The RPD then analyzed the appellant's explanation, and in its decision, it explained why it was found unsatisfactory: the appellant prepared a very detailed modified version of her BOC Form after realizing that her allegations were incomplete, and it is therefore not credible that she would have omitted such serious allegations in the amended version. The RPD found that the appellant's credibility was undermined. I agree with this analysis.

In my opinion, not only did the appellant omit important information from her BOC Form, including from the amendments, but she also gave the panel a completely different version of the facts and events at the heart of her claim for refugee protection in Canada. The omissions and contradictions are serious and relate to her fear of returning to Haiti. I consider her answer-putting the blame on the translator- unsatisfactory. What is more, by signing her BOC Form, she declared that the entire content of it and all attached documents were interpreted to her. I note that her BOC Form also contains the declaration signed by the interpreter stating that he accurately interpreted the entire content of the form and all attached documents for the claimant from French to Creole. He declares that he is proficient in both languages and was able to communicate effectively with the appellant, who assured him that she understood the entire content of the form and all attached documents and the answers provided, as interpreted by him. Considering the importance of the omitted facts, which at the heart of her fear of returning to Haiti, and the contradictions raised, I find the appellant's credibility to be seriously undermined.

The RPD also raised other contradictions in the appellant's account. In her BOC Form, the appellant states that she did not return to Haiti after leaving the country in 2009. In the amendments submitted three days prior to her hearing before the RPD, she states that she returned there on XXXX XXXX, 2014. At the hearing, she testified that she also returned in 2012 and 2013 to visit her family and husband.

The appellant states that the RPD did not take her explanations concerning the reasons for changing her BOC Form into account, namely, errors made by the appellant's first counsel and the interpreter's bad translation. With all due respect to the appellant, I disagree. On the contrary, the RPD confronted her about the three versions given about her round trips to Haiti and took into account her explanations blaming her former counsel for putting information that she did not recognize in her BOC Form.5 Nevertheless, the RPD did not consider that answer reasonable.

I agree that this answer is an unsatisfactory explanation for why the appellant contradicted herself three times rather than once on such a basic and significant aspect of her account for the following reasons. The appellant has been represented her current counsel since December 19, 2017, long before her hearing before the RPD on September 20, 2018. Three days prior to her hearing, she presented the RPD with the amendments to her BOC Form and, at the beginning of the hearing, she confirmed that besides the changes made, the information in her BOC Form is true, complete and correct. In this context, I consider that blaming her previous counsel, from before December 2017, is not a satisfactory explanation. I find that the appellant's credibility is undermined by these contradictions. I do not see any error in the RPD's analysis and findings.

Furthermore, while the RPD noted that the appellant did not follow the procedures stated in the practice notice issued by the Chairperson of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB), setting out the steps to follow when the person who is the subject of an IRB proceeding alleges that they were inadequately represented by a former counsel, it is clear that this is still the case.6 The appellant argues in her memorandum that the purpose of the practice notice is to help members to carry out their decision-making duties and to promote consistency, coherence and fairness in the IRB's treatment of cases. She states that she filed a very detailed amended modified version of her BOC Form in order to amend the BOC Form that had been prepared, translated and filed by her former counsel. Nevertheless, in her memorandum, she fails to provide any information showing that she followed the procedure stated in the practice notice, a central part of which is the obligation to inform her former counsel, in writing, about the allegations against him and give him the opportunity to address them.

The RPD also noted the fact that the appellant states in her BOC Form that, in 2015, she stopped paying the police when she stopped sending money to her family in Haiti to be given to the police. However, at the hearing, she contradicted herself, testifying that her mother stopped paying in XXXX 2018. The RPD brought the contradiction to the appellant's attention and gave her the chance to explain. Once again, the appellant blamed her former counsel and the translator, stating that the translator had translated the counsel's story. For the same reasons given above in relation to the contradictions regarding the times she was in Haiti, I consider this answer unsatisfactory in explaining why the appellant contradicted herself on such a key part of her story, that is, paying the police who were extorting her. Moreover, there is a substantial difference, calculating in years, between when she stopped paying her extortionists, that is, between 2015 and 2018. In these circumstances, I find the appellant's credibility to be further undermined.

In my opinion, given the significance of the omissions and contradictions mentioned so far and given that they are at the heart of her claim for refugee protection and her alleged fear of returning to Haiti, I consider them sufficient to conclude that the appellant's allegations about her violent confrontations with her husband and his involvement in the police's extortion attempts are not credible. Expedited analysis

The appellant states that the RPD's analysis of the testimonial evidence and documentation was expeditious in order to conclude that there is no risk to her life and physical integrity in Haiti, that it did not take the time to do its duty in assessing of the facts and that it did not take all the evidence into account. I do not agree.

The evidence on the record comes down to the appellant's statements in her BOC Form, the amendments made to it three days prior to the hearing and the documents contained in the National Documentation Package on Haiti regarding the living conditions in that country, including for Haitian women. As the above analysis shows, the RPD took all these elements into account when evaluating the appellant's refugee protection claim. In my opinion, considering all the evidence on the record and because of the numerous credibility issues noted and analyzed above, I find that the appellant is not credible and that she did not establish that she would face any risk of returning to Haiti. Stress during the hearing

The appellant claims that the RPD did not take into account the stress that she could have experienced during her hearing. The appellant notes in her memorandum that having to appear at a hearing before the IRB can be difficult because of language and cultural barriers and the importance of the outcome of the hearing for refugee protection claimants.

I understand that the appellant might have been stressed during her hearing before the RPD. Nevertheless, her record does not contain a psychological or medical report mentioning any inability to testify. In her memorandum, the appellant does not mention that there were interpretation issues during her hearing before the RPD. In addition, the recording of the hearing reveals that the appellant understood the interpreter, which she also confirmed at the beginning of the hearing, and does not reveal that she had any problems testifying. I note that the RPD demonstrated courtesy when questioning the appellant. The RPD even also took a break during the hearing and encouraged the appellant to ask for another break if she needed one.7 Above all, I am of the opinion that the RPD provided the appellant with all the latitude needed to explain herself.

Overall, although I understand that the appellant might have experienced some stress during her RPD hearing, it is my opinion that the stress cannot account for the contradictions, omissions and inconsistencies identified revealed and analyzed above. Possibility of gender-related persecution

The RPD analyzed the appellant's refugee protection claim in light of section 96. The appellant does not challenge the analysis. After conducting my own analysis, I am of the opinion that the RPD's conclusion that the appellant did not show that she faces a serious risk of persecution in Haiti by reason of her membership in the particular social group of Haitian women is correct.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD's determination that the appellant, XXXX XXXX, is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
